examples.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1] \times [0,1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/c3c2b2e7a9d5b2b8f76499b0ad62d628f9d79bc7c41b6bcaf9926df4f368cdbf.png)
Find the matrix equation that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $\big[ 1, \: 1 \big]^T,$ and compute the components of the first iteration.
examples.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_n) = -\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x & -2y \\ 2y & 2x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/13f9eb9850462317be5a5c7da22fe53ee89b24d9ce1a9226c2d0ee1e6355ba19.png)

Starting with ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/8bdb55b26b462507d9810675499558be66e7b970d2f9fdb78e708807e617ce8d.png) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}2x & -2y \\ 2y & 2x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\ 2xy-1\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}2(1) & -2(1) \\ 2(1) & 2(1)\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}(1)^{2}-(1)^{2} \\ 2(1)(1)-1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/d5eb5a91fdd96bf6ca50539d2119a97ce9e5600b3114f708cda4d95a047e8b81.png) Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+[\begin{aligned}-0.25 \\ -0.25\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-0.25 \\ -0.25\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.75 \\ 0.75\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-3,0]\times [0,3]⊆{R}^{2},$ where

$$
f(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3 \\ {x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1\end{aligned}].
$$

Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,0]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[-3,\,3]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).

| ${x}_{2}\,≈[$ | $-2.621$ | $]$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| {{field-1}} |  |  |
feedback.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{3}-1 & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3} \\ 3{x}^{2}-2y & -2x+2y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{3}-1 & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3} \\ 3{x}^{2}-2y & -2x+2y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3 \\ {x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{3}-1 & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3} \\ 3{x}^{2}-2y & -2x+2y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3 \\ {x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2(-3)(3)^{3}-1 & 3(-3)^{2}(3)^{2}+4(3)^{3} \\ 3(-3)^{2}-2(3) & -2(-3)+2(3)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}(-3)^{2}(3)^{3}-(-3)+{3}^{4}-3 \\ (-3)^{3}-2(-3)(3)+{3}^{2}+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}-163 & 351 \\ 21 & 12\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}324 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{(-163)\cdot 12-351\cdot 21}[\begin{aligned}12 & -351 \\ -21 & -163\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}324 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{9327}[\begin{aligned}3537 \\ -6967\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}-2.621 \\ 2.253\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.
